planting.note: Plant dormant corms or container-grown stock in fall (when the winter leaf naturally appears) in moist, acidic, humus-rich, loose leaf-litter soil in deep to partial shade; cranefly orchid depends on an undisturbed mycorrhizal fungal partner in the soil and transplants poorly bare-root — use only nursery-propagated material, never wild-collected plants.

directions: Site in moist, humus-rich, undisturbed leaf-litter soil in deep to partial shade beneath hardwoods; do not rake or disturb the leaf litter over the planting, and never dig plants from the wild. Tipularia discolor is one of the most unusual native orchids of eastern deciduous forests, with a two-phase life cycle that separates its leaf and flower entirely: a single dark green, purple-spotted, pleated leaf emerges in fall and persists through winter, photosynthesizing during the leafless dormant season, then withers away in spring before the summer flower spike — a slender raceme of small, translucent greenish-purple, oddly asymmetric flowers pollinated at night by noctuid moths — rises leafless from the same corm. Because the leaf and bloom never overlap, the plant is easy to overlook except in winter, when its solitary spotted leaf stands out against bare forest floor. A genuinely distinctive conversation piece for a shaded native woodland garden in zone 5–9, best left undisturbed once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; heartleaf aster is one of the few asters that thrives and flowers reliably under deciduous trees, spreading gently by rhizomes and self-sown seedlings.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; pinch or shear by half in early summer to keep the habit compact and floriferous. Symphyotrichum cordifolium (heartleaf or blue wood aster) is a native woodland perennial named for its heart-shaped, toothed lower leaves, sending up airy, branching sprays of small, pale blue-to-lavender, yellow-centered daisies in late summer and fall — exactly when few other shade plants are blooming, making it a critical late-season nectar source for native bees and migrating butterflies. It naturalizes readily under high canopy trees and along woodland edges, spreading by shallow rhizomes and light self-seeding without becoming aggressive in cultivated beds. Combine with ferns, sedges, and other shade perennials for a naturalistic fall display in zone 3–8.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or late winter in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial sun; Florida flame azalea is native to Gulf South ravines and stream bluffs and resents heavy, poorly drained clay — mound or amend planting sites on wet sites.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon protection; mulch well to keep roots cool and never let the root zone dry out completely in the first two seasons. Rhododendron austrinum is a deciduous native azalea of the Gulf Coastal Plain — from the Florida panhandle and south Georgia west into Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana — prized as one of the most fragrant of all native azaleas. In early to mid-spring, before or as the leaves emerge, the shrub is smothered in large trusses of intensely honeysuckle-scented flowers ranging from clear yellow through orange to deep gold-orange, drawing in early spring pollinators including native bees and swallowtail butterflies. It naturally colonizes the dappled shade of bluffs, ravines, and stream banks under a high pine and hardwood canopy. Excellent as a specimen or in a woodland-edge shrub border in the Gulf South, where it is far better adapted to summer heat and humidity than most Asian azalea hybrids. Zone 7–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Mount Cuba Center — Native Azalea Research

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost (cold-moist stratify 3–4 weeks for best germination) and transplant out after frost, or divide established clumps in spring or fall, into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near pond edges, rain gardens, or low woodland spots; does not tolerate prolonged drought. Scutellaria lateriflora (mad-dog skullcap) is a native wetland and streamside perennial in the mint family, grown for its small blue-to-violet, two-lipped flowers that line the leaf axils in a distinctive one-sided (lateriflora) arrangement, and for the aerial parts, which are harvested at flowering and dried for traditional calming herbal preparations. Despite the common name, the plant is not associated with rabies — the name stems from historical folk use as a treatment for rabid-animal bites. It spreads by rhizomes into loose colonies in reliably damp ground and is a good choice for the moist partial-shade margins of a rain garden or bog bed, where it also attracts small native bees. Zone 3–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; hearts-a-bustin' is an understory shrub of moist hardwood forests and needs consistent soil moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun, especially in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly watered, especially through the first two summers, and protect from deer, which browse the foliage and stems readily. Euonymus americanus is an open, airy, native deciduous shrub of eastern woodlands, grown chiefly for its remarkable fruit display: in fall, warty, bright crimson-pink seed capsules split open to reveal glossy orange-red seeds dangling on threads, giving rise to the descriptive common name 'hearts-a-bustin'.' Small, inconspicuous, greenish-white flowers appear in late spring, easy to overlook until the dramatic fruit show follows in September and October. The slender green stems provide winter interest and mild color even when bare. Best used as a specimen at the edge of a shaded woodland garden or native plant border where the fall fruit display can be appreciated up close, in zone 6–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
